lead: Instruments a person owns to look at the sky, nature and the very small, and to measure weather and the world at home: telescopes and their mounts and accessories, binoculars and night optics, microscopes and magnifiers, weather and Earth instruments, sky models and historic instruments, and a home and hobby lab; organised by what you observe, with icons as archetypes at the enthusiast end and restraint at the utility end.
ax: What is it for: looking at the sky, at distant things on land, at the very small, reading the weather and ground, modelling or finding stars, or working with samples at a bench; and is it the instrument or a part that fits one?
key: 1. Is it a part, tool or sensor that fits a telescope (mount, eyepiece, camera, filter, collimator)? → Telescope mounts & accessories
2. Does it gather light from the sky for you to look into on its own (refractor, reflector, catadioptric, smart, solar)? → Telescopes
3. Is it a viewer for distant things on land or for the dark (binoculars, monocular, spotting scope, night vision)? → Binoculars & spotting scopes
4. Does it enlarge small things, with a microscope stand or a lens held to the eye? → Microscopes & magnifiers
5. Does it read the weather, air pressure, radiation or ground movement? → Weather & Earth instruments
6. Is it a model of the sky or an old star-finding or navigating instrument? → Sky models & historic instruments
7. Is it glassware, a bench device or a kit for working on samples? → Home & hobby lab

Precedence: a camera or filter made for a telescope is a telescope accessory (step 1) before a microscope camera (step 4); a low-vision magnifier → H2; a night-vision weapon sight → E4; a celestial globe sold as a map object → F1.

depts.note: Home weather stations are tier; barometers and weather glasses are collected and are variety, with antique forms as a period view.
depts.t: Instruments a person keeps to read the weather, air pressure, radiation and ground movement at home; a barometer built into a clock → A5; a room air-quality monitor → B7.
depts.ax: What does it read: the weather near the ground, the air pressure, or the ground and radiation?

k.a: home weather station · personal weather station
k.d: Set of instruments that measures several weather quantities together and shows or uploads the readings.

x.d: Solar-powered, console-free all-in-one station (2020) with a haptic rain sensor and lightning detection, read through an app.
Davis's reference home weather station, on the market for about two decades and long rated the most accurate consumer station.
x.dt: cabled or wireless · standard or fan-aspirated shield · cup or sonic anemometer

x.d: Smaller, cheaper Davis all-in-one station with compact shielding and lesser sensors than the Pro2.

k.d: Instrument that reads the air temperature indoors or outdoors.
Sealed column of liquid with weighted glass bulbs that rise or sink with temperature, each tagged with a reading.

x.d: Floating-bulb thermometer devised by the Accademia del Cimento in Florence and described in 1666; revived as a decorative piece from the 1990s.

v.d: sold by the Natural History Museum, London

x.dt: column height · number of bulbs · coloured liquids

k.d: Instrument that reads the humidity of the air, usually with temperature too.
Instrument that measures wind speed.

x.d: Waterproof handheld impeller wind meter designed in 1995 by Nielsen-Kellerman's co-founder for gliding; the reference pocket anemometer.

k.d: Instrument that collects and measures rainfall.

x.d: High-capacity 4-inch manual gauge required for CoCoRaHS volunteer reports; catches within a few per cent of the US NWS 8-inch standard gauge.

k.d: Instrument that logs the hours of bright sunshine in a day, by burning a card, exposing paper or sensing light; a classic of weather-station collecting.
tt: Burn card behind a glass sphere

x.d: Glass sphere that focuses sunlight to burn a trace on a card; improved by Stokes in 1879.

k.d: Receiver that senses the radio pulse of lightning to warn of an approaching storm; sold as a stand-alone unit or a weather-station add-on.
White louvred box that shelters a thermometer and hygrometer from sun and rain so they read true air temperature.

s.t: Instruments that show air pressure and the weather it forecasts, from antique mercury sticks to a storm glass; a station with a pressure sensor → Weather stations & sensors.
s.ax: kinds by how pressure is shown: a pointer or column, a chart line, or crystals in a glass

k.d: Instrument that shows air pressure, and so the likely weather, with a mercury column or a sealed aneroid capsule.

x.d: Upright mercury-tube barometer in a narrow case, the original form after Torricelli's 1643 experiment.

v.d: adjustable mercury cistern for exact readings, named after Jean Nicolas Fortin

x.dt: mahogany or oak case · cistern or siphon tube · vernier scale

x.d: Mercury barometer whose float turns a pointer round a dial, in a banjo-shaped case; popular in Britain from about 1810.
x.dt: banjo case · dial with weather words · often with thermometer and hygrometer

x.d: Barometer using a sealed metal capsule instead of liquid, invented by Lucien Vidi in 1844; the common household form.

v.d: Short & Mason with Taylor Instrument Companies

x.dt: brass or wood case · dial · ship's-wheel and porthole styles

x.d: Mercury barometer with thermometers and printed rules for forecasting, after Admiral Robert FitzRoy; made for homes after his death in 1865.

v.d: oak case, dry and wet thermometers

x.d: Gimballed mercury barometer with an iron cistern that became the standard on Royal Navy and other ships in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
x.dt: brass tube · iron cistern · gimbals · attached thermometer

k.d: Barometer that records air pressure over time as a line on a paper chart turned by clockwork.

x.d: Recording barometer from the Paris firm of Jules and Max Richard, whose 1880s recorders set the pattern; marked with the RF monogram.

k.a: chemical weather glass · FitzRoy's storm barometer
k.d: Sealed glass of camphor solution whose crystals were believed to foretell the weather; really a crude thermoscope.

x.d: Storm glass popularised in the 1860s by Admiral Robert FitzRoy, after the Crown gave them to fishing communities following the 1859 storms.
x.dt: camphor, potassium nitrate, ammonium chloride in ethanol and water

s.t: Small instruments that detect ionising radiation or ground motion at home, such as a Geiger counter or a Raspberry Shake.

k.d: Handheld detector that counts ionising radiation and shows a dose rate, used by hobbyists, collectors and preppers.

x.d: Budget Geiger counter family from GQ Electronics, the common hobby entry point.
Open-source, GPS-logging radiation kit for mapping from a car or bike, the workhorse of the Safecast citizen network.

k.d: Small seismograph run at home that records earthquakes and local ground motion and can share data with a citizen network.

x.d: Raspberry Pi-based home seismograph whose owners form a live citizen seismic network.

depts.note: Models of the sky and classic observing and navigation instruments, collected new and antique; period is a view across them.
depts.t: Models of the sky and old instruments for finding stars, time and position, collected new or antique; a telescope → Telescopes; a terrestrial globe → F1; a clock or sundial → A5.
depts.ax: Does it show the sky as a model to look at, or is it used to find stars, time and position?

s.t: Display models of the heavens: orrery, armillary sphere, celestial globe or a home planetarium projector; a hand instrument for finding stars → Star finders & navigation instruments.
s.ax: kinds by what is modelled: planets in motion, the sky as rings, the stars on a sphere, the sky projected on a ceiling

k.d: Mechanical model of the Sun, planets and moons, turned by hand, clockwork or motor.

x.d: The first orreries: George Graham's planetary machine, copied and improved by John Rowley for the Earl of Orrery, who gave the device its name.

v.d: made for Charles Boyle, 4th Earl of Orrery

x.d: Orrery after the new planetary model Benjamin Martin devised in 1764; a 1766 example was used at Harvard.
American classroom tellurion showing Sun, Earth, Moon and Venus with seasons, phases and eclipses, made in Michigan since the early 20th century.
x.dt: maple, ebonised, Bakelite or plastic arm · hand-cranked or electric

k.d: Model of the sky made of rings for the celestial equator, ecliptic and other circles around a central Earth or Sun.
Globe showing the stars and constellations on the celestial sphere, usually mounted with meridian and horizon rings.

x.d: Willem Jansz Blaeu's engraved celestial globes from Amsterdam, first based on Tycho Brahe's star catalogue; among the finest of 17th-century Europe.
x.dt: engraved gores · brass meridian · wooden stand

x.d: Georgian library globe from J. & W. Cary of the Strand, the leading British globe makers of the 19th century.
Modern celestial globes from Replogle, the Chicago globe maker founded in 1930.

k.d: Small projector that shows the night sky on the ceiling and walls of a room.

x.d: The first home optical planetarium, developed by Takayuki Ohira with Sega Toys in 2005; about 1.7 million sold by 2021.

s.t: Hand instruments that find stars, tell the time by them or measure a star's height, such as an astrolabe, a planisphere or a sextant; a display model → Sky models.
s.ax: kinds by what is read off: stars and time (planisphere, astrolabe, nocturnal), or an angle above the horizon (quadrant, backstaff, sextant)

k.d: Pair of rotating discs that show which stars are above the horizon at any date and time for one latitude.

x.d: Two-sided planisphere with separate north- and south-facing maps that removes most distortion; first printed in 1976.
The best-known British planisphere, set for latitude 51.5° N.
Planisphere by Storm Dunlop and Wil Tirion, approved by the Royal Observatory Greenwich.

k.d: Hand-held instrument that models the sky, used to find star and Sun positions, the time and latitude.

x.d: Astrolabe usable at any latitude without changing plates, perfected by Ibn al-Sarraj of Aleppo.
Classic astrolabe: a mater holding latitude plates (tympans) under a rotating star map (rete), with a sighting alidade on the back; Greek in origin, refined in the Islamic world.
x.dt: mater · tympans for latitudes · rete · alidade · brass

x.d: Astrolabe adapted for use on a ship's heaving deck; a simplified form was promoted by Prince Henry the Navigator.

k.d: Hand dial that tells the time at night by lining a pointer up with Polaris and a guard star; a navigators' timepiece, sold today as brass reproductions.
see: time from the sun instead of the stars

k.d: Quarter-circle instrument that measures the angle of a star or the Sun above the horizon with a plumb line or sights; pocket and observatory forms.

x.d: Pocket quadrant carrying projections of the tropics, equator and horizon, used to find time and day length.

k.d: Navigator's instrument that measures the Sun's height by the shadow it casts, so the user faces away from the Sun; replaced by the octant.

x.d: Backstaff with a small and a large arc, the form most identified with the instrument.
Late backstaff variant of the Davis quadrant.

k.d: Double-reflecting hand instrument that measures the angle between a celestial body and the horizon for navigation.

x.d: John Hadley's double-reflecting instrument of about 1731 (also found by Thomas Godfrey), the ancestor of the sextant.
German micrometer-drum sextant with a bronze frame, made by Cassens & Plath of Bremen from 1962, often sold through Weems & Plath.
x.dt: bronze frame · black enamel · micrometer drum

x.d: Plastic micrometer-drum sextant sold as a low-cost learner and backup instrument.

Metal rod on a base with rings and clamps that hold glassware above a heater.
